old_entry.title: Capcom
old_entry.subtitle: Capcom Builds a Game Culture Through Systems That Can Be Refined
old_entry.summary: Capcom lists May 30, 1979 as its establishment date.
body: Capcom lists May 30, 1979 as its establishment date. From arcades to consoles, the company would build some of the industry's most influential series: Street Fighter, Mega Man, Resident Evil, Monster Hunter, Devil May Cry and many others. The common thread is not one genre, but strong attention to control, repeatability and systems that can be learned deeply. Capcom moves through crises and transformations, yet repeatedly returns to its own ideas and rewrites them through new technology, audiences and forms of distribution.

The original companies that spawned Capcom's Japan branch were I.R.M. and its subsidiary Japan Capsule Computers Co., Ltd., both of which were devoted to the manufacture and distribution of electronic game machines. The two companies underwent a name change to Sanbi Co., Ltd. in September 1981. On June 11, 1983, Tsujimoto established Capcom Co., Ltd. to take over the internal sales department.

Street Fighter II turns the fighting game into a system of distinct characters, special moves, spacing and timing. Its success does not come only from a charismatic roster. One-on-one matches create situations repeatable enough to study and variable enough to remain tense. Arcades and home conversions spread a common vocabulary of combos, matchups and space control. For Capcom, competitive play demonstrates the strength of systems that can be understood quickly yet refined for years, a philosophy that continues to influence later productions.

With Resident Evil, Capcom redirects part of its experience toward the slower rhythm of horror. Ammunition, healing, inventory space and saves become resources that force planning. Fixed camera angles and pre-rendered environments do more than display detailed graphics: they control what the player can see and therefore what can be feared. The series' success demonstrates that Capcom's systemic precision can work in a genre opposite to arcade action. Tension emerges precisely by limiting what the player can do safely.

The company emerged within Japanese electronic entertainment and grew as arcades became a rapid laboratory for rules, difficulty and visual attraction. In that market, every game had to communicate immediately and persuade the audience to try again. This pressure contributed to a design culture attentive to control response and readability. Many skills Capcom later brought to consoles were refined in an environment where player feedback was direct, public and measurable. This passage explains why Capcom remains interesting beyond its date. corporate origins and arcades is not isolated, but a node connecting production, rules and player perception inside the same experience.

old_entry.title: Inti Creates
old_entry.subtitle: Inti Creates and the Art of Making Classic 2D Feel Modern
old_entry.summary: Inti Creates was founded on May 8, 1996.
body: Inti Creates was founded on May 8, 1996. The studio would cross multiple hardware generations while preserving a specific expertise: translating the rhythm of 2D action into readable, responsive systems suited to different machines. From work on Mega Man Zero and ZX to original projects such as Azure Striker Gunvolt and Blaster Master Zero, its history shows that pixel art is not necessarily nostalgia. It can be a production and design choice able to evolve alongside controls, displays and audience expectations.

Inti Creates was established in Japan in 1996 and grew through projects where animation, collision and control response had to remain readable even on small screens. Specialization did not mean immobility. The studio learned to change resolutions, palettes, memory formats and input devices without losing one constant principle: action must communicate cause and effect immediately. That discipline made the team especially suited to series demanding strict rhythm and characters recognizable within only a few frames.

With Mega Man Zero, Inti Creates moved a home-console series into the constraints of Game Boy Advance. The smaller screen forced reconsideration of sprite size, danger distance and reading speed. The result emphasizes aggressive movement, close combat and sharp animation. Difficulty is not ornamental; it emerges from the density with which enemies, platforms and attacks enter the visible space. The studio therefore turns a hardware limitation into a faster, sharper identity.

Azure Striker Gunvolt shows how Inti Creates can begin with run-and-gun tradition and alter its logic. Players tag targets and use Gunvolt's electricity to damage them continuously while energy, mobility and risk interact. Shooting is no longer only a matter of pressing accurately at the right moment. It means building a temporary relationship between character and enemies. This changes combat rhythm and shows a studio interested in preserving 2D clarity without simply repeating systems from the past.

old_entry.title: The artist between a drawing and a display
old_entry.summary: What does remaking early Final Fantasy pixel art reveal about its original making?
body: Kazuko Shibuya recalls redrawing the first Final Fantasy's prologue landscape as silhouettes to fit limited memory. The picture appeared when the player crossed the bridge; it was not an unused scene. When she recreated it for Pixel Remaster, the original digital data was unavailable. A printout she had kept supplied a reference. This makes preservation tangible. A paper copy of released artwork helped its original artist return to earlier decisions. The surviving sheet and the later redraw belong to different moments, and both need clear dates and captions.

In the same interview, Shibuya discusses how colour behaved on older cathode-ray-tube displays, in contrast with the sharply separated pixels of modern screens. Redrawing an early character is therefore not just a matter of counting squares. The display is part of how neighbouring colours become an image. This gives the remaster an artistic problem rather than a simple instruction to make everything sharper. A comparison should identify both the edition and the viewing conditions, so the museum does not confuse a modern enlargement with the appearance of the original hardware.

Koichi Ishii's account of the first Final Fantasy describes a production arrangement involving Shibuya, Takashi Tokita and himself. While Shibuya was occupied with other work, Tokita helped Ishii learn the sprite tools, and Ishii worked on the side-view battle presentation. Such recollections complicate a convenient single-artist story. A recognisable character can pass through design, tool learning, input and revision before it reaches the screen. The interview makes those handovers worth naming. Crediting Shibuya's contribution does not require assigning every early Final Fantasy pixel to her alone.

Square Enix's Pixel Remaster FAQ identifies Shibuya with the redrawn character graphics and describes an effort to keep the feel of the earlier games. It separately identifies the illustration galleries and Yoshitaka Amano's concept art. Those distinctions matter when different kinds of art appear together in one exhibit. A concept illustration, an original sprite and a later redraw are related objects, not interchangeable versions of a single file. The 2021 project gives the museum a reason to compare them while preserving the authorship and date of each contribution.
